tagline.text: A tall Negros waterfall falling like cigarette smoke in a highland forest

location.label: Location
location.text: Brgy. Kumaliskis, Don Salvador Benedicto, Negros Occidental (trek from the Malatan-og View Deck)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,200 (day trip from Bacolod, including transport, entrance fee, guide and food)

children.text: Malatan-og Falls is a forest waterfall in Don Salvador Benedicto, a little over an hour from Bacolod by bus. After registering at the view deck, you walk down with a guide for 30 to 45 minutes to a cold pool, passing coffee fields and small rice terraces on the way.

Malatan-og Falls is a waterfall in Barangay Kumaliskis, Don Salvador Benedicto (DSB for short), Negros Occidental. Its long, thin stream breaks into spray as it falls, which earned it the nickname "Cigarette Falls," and local guides describe it as the tallest waterfall in Negros Occidental. Sources do not agree on the exact drop, so this guide gives no figure.

DSB is a highland area inside the Northern Negros Natural Park. Away from Bacolod's heat, you get cool pine forests and coffee fields, and the water in the falls' pool is icy cold. That makes it a good nature day to carve out of a Bacolod city itinerary. The DSB area averages roughly 700 m above sea level and the falls viewpoint is reported at about 870 m, and it is clearly cooler than Bacolod, enough that you may want a light long-sleeved layer on a rainy day. It adds forest and waterfall scenery to a Negros trip that is otherwise mostly about beaches.

The plan is simple. At the Malatan-og View Deck beside the highway, take photos, register as a visitor, pay the entrance fee and get a guide assigned. Then walk down stairs, a forest path, coffee fields and a stream section to the base of the falls. The walk down takes about
30–45 minutes
, and the climb back is much harder, so plan on roughly twice the descent time.

Going with a guide is the basic rule here. Local residents show the way and look after your safety, and the entrance and guide fees help sustain village tourism. It takes some fitness but there is no rock climbing, so families with sturdy shoes and plenty of time can do it. If you are carrying a small child or heavy bags, the trek will be tiring, so pack light and bring just a towel and a change of clothes in one waterproof bag. Please confirm current local guidance and fees before you go.
The long, thin stream drops along the rock face and scatters into spray. Standing close, you feel a fine mist on your face. After rain the flow grows and the falls look more powerful.

From the deck beside the highway you can look across the valley at the falls and the mountains. You can take photos even if you skip the trek, and this is also where you register and pay. The railing area is steep, so take care.
The trail starts with gravel steps and a forest path, with a resting hut along the way. Thanks to the cool highland air and tree shade, it feels less hot than you might expect.

blocks.title: Coffee fields and small rice terraces

children.text: Midway the forest opens up to coffee farms and small rice terraces. This stretch makes the scenery more varied than a trip to see only the falls.
Near the falls you walk along the stream and cross it several times. Wet rocks are slippery, so this is the part to be careful with, but it feels like a real adventure and stays in the memory.

You can swim in the pool below the falls. The water is very cold, so you will not stay long, and it works best as a natural cold dip to cool down after the walk. Be sure to bring a change of clothes and a towel.
Guides are village residents who show the way and can tell you about nearby plants and local stories. Some visitors report tipping the guide separately.
Pine forests, ziplines, viewpoints and small rice terraces are described along the same road. If you have time after the falls, you can add one or two of them.

items.title: Day trip course
items.subtitle: From Bacolod to the falls via the view deck

children.text: Take a bus toward San Carlos from the Bacolod South Bus Terminal (Ceres South Terminal). Tell the driver beforehand that you are getting off at the Malatan-og View Deck.
Arrive at the Malatan-og View Deck, take photos, then write your name at the information desk, pay the entrance fee and get a guide.
Walk down with your guide along the stairs and forest path. Pass the coffee fields and rice terraces and catch your breath at the resting hut.
Cross the stream, follow the rocky path and reach the falls. Take photos and swim in the pool.
Start back, leaving plenty of time for the climb. The ascent is hard, so walk slowly and rest.
Eat lunch at a restaurant or stall near the view deck and buy snacks and local specialties.
Wait on the highway for a bus back to Bacolod. Buses reportedly come about once an hour, so leave before dark.
Bus schedules and last departure times can change, so ask the view deck staff about the ride back. Bus times and availability vary with local conditions.
Leave Bacolod early and aim to reach the Malatan-og View Deck.
Finish the falls trek first. The morning has better weather and less slippery trails.
Come back up, have lunch and rest.
If you have time and energy left, make a light stop at a pine forest, zipline or viewpoint around DSB. Check locally whether it is operating.
Catch a ride back to Bacolod before sunset.
The highland road gets dark and can be foggy after sunset, so avoid traveling late.
There are direct flights from Manila (MNL) to Bacolod-Silay International Airport (BCD). The flight takes about
1 hour 10~30 minutes
, and schedules and fares vary by airline, so check when you book.
From the airport, take a taxi or van into Bacolod city and then go on to the South Bus Terminal. Depending on your arrival time, you can rest in the city and start the next morning.
You can also reach Negros by boat and road from Cebu or Iloilo.
Take a bus toward San Carlos from the Bacolod South Bus Terminal (Ceres) and get off at the Malatan-og View Deck. It takes about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes
, and the air-conditioned fare is reported at about
For the return, wait on the highway for a bus to Bacolod. Reports say one passes about once an hour, so allow some slack.
To avoid missing your stop, tell the driver in advance and save the Malatan-og View Deck on Google Maps so you can check your position.
Jeepneys to Don Salvador are reported to leave from near Libertad Market in Bacolod, at about
, but sources differ widely (2020 blog; confirm locally). The last trip can be around 3 p.m., so be sure to confirm your ride back.
Private cars and rental cars can park along the highway. Head for the view deck near coordinates 10.5939, 123.2277.
The highland road is hilly, so cycling is recommended only for experienced riders.

In the dry season the trail is less slippery and the stream is easier to cross, so it suits trekking. This guide treats roughly November to May as the dry season, but it varies by year, so check the weather before you go.

In the rainy season the flow grows and the falls look more imposing. But hiking becomes dangerous in rain, and mosquitoes, mud and rising streams are problems, so it is safest not to go on rainy days or right after rain.

Even on the same day, mornings usually have fewer clouds and drier trails. Afternoon showers are common in the highlands, so an early start is recommended. Weekends and holidays can bring more visitors.

Staying overnight in DSB is less convenient than basing yourself in Bacolod and making a day trip. Bacolod has plenty of hotels and restaurants, so getting around and eating is easy. If you want a night in the highlands, lodge-style resorts on the San Carlos side are mentioned, but check their location and facilities before booking.

Near the view deck there are restaurants serving simple meals and snack stalls, and some vendors sell wild honey and local goods. But there are almost no shops along the falls trail itself, so bring water and snacks before you set off. One reviewer-recommended spot nearby is Busay Balay.

To get up early from Bacolod, choose a hotel near the South Bus Terminal or the city center. Have lunch near the view deck, and for dinner return to Bacolod and eat chicken inasal, a local favorite, or another restaurant in the city. You will be tired after the falls, so do not plan a late evening.
Pay the entrance fee at the view deck, write your name and go down with a guide. Reports say you may not go alone.
Bring non-slip shoes and, if possible, hiking sticks. There are many wet rocks.
If the walk down takes
30–45 minutes
, plan on about twice that for the climb back.
Bring a change of clothes, a towel and a waterproof bag to make things easier after swimming.
Insect repellent and long pants reduce mosquito bites and scratches from leaves.
Carry plenty of cash. Cards or e-payments may not work.
Ask at the view deck about the last bus back to Bacolod.
Fees and rules can change, so check the latest notice from the DSB tourism office.
Bring at least a liter of water and simple snacks. There are reportedly almost no shops along the trail.
Do not trek during rain or right after it, because the stream and rocks are very slippery and the water rises.
Going down is easy but the climb back is much harder. Pace yourself and walk slowly to save energy and time.
The pool is very cold. Do not stay in long, and do not jump from the rocks.
It is easy to slip at stream crossings and on wet rocks, so follow your guide's directions.
The view deck railing area is steep, so watch children closely.
The highland road is dark and can be foggy after sunset, so do not stay late.
The starting and return base, about
1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes
by bus, with plenty of restaurants and hotels.
Pine forests and viewpoints are described along the same highland road. Check locally whether they are open.
